scope: Frozen, manually selected 60-query benchmark of the exact text contents of four checked-in Knowhere demo documents. Development uses only the Transformers tutorial document family; held-out queries use the two dated Micron investor presentations and the SpaceX S-1. This is a small diverse within-repository sample, not a sample representative of production traffic. Gold is prepared before model outputs. The live experiment derives a text-only corpus from existing page.content; original PDF interpretation, images, and visual table understanding are outside scope. Proof chunk IDs and SHA256 hashes refer to original source records; evaluation must follow any deterministic derived-chunk mapping and verify actual final-visible text, never count an original source ID alone as coverage. All quotes in one proof are jointly required; multiple proofs are alternatives. Questions classified unanswerable have at least one deliberately unavailable facet; related disclosed facts do not satisfy that facet. Dates distinguish historical facts, changed guidance, and forecasts.

questions.query: In the tutorial, how is an initial composite representation built, how does it become context-aware, and how do tokens exchange information through attention?

requirements.text: Tokenize the composite and embed each token as a vector.

quotes:
Tokenize the composite (divide it into tokens).
2.
Embed each of the token as a vector.

requirements.text: Feed the representation through several transformer layers to obtain context-aware embeddings.

quotes:
Feed the representation through several transformer layers to 
obtain “context-aware” embeddings.

requirements.text: Each token sends messages to other tokens and uses attention to weight those messages when moving its embedding.

quotes:
Each token sends a message to every other token.
2.
Each token computes how much does it want to take into account the 
messages of each other token. This is the idea of attention.
3.
Each token moves away from his embedding in the direction signaled 
by the message of each other token weighted by the attention that he is 
paying to that token.

Falcon 9. As the world’s first orbital-class rapidly reusable rocket, Falcon 9 was first launched in 2010 and has 
a payload capacity to LEO of approximately 23 metric tons when fully expendable. Falcon 9 has completed 
approximately 620 orbital space launches as of March 31, 2026, and an over 99% mission success rate.

requirements.text: Falcon Heavy first launched in 2018, has approximately 64 metric tons LEO capacity, and a 100% mission success rate from 11 launches as of March 31, 2026.

Roadster”) and its mannequin passenger, known as Starman, into orbit around the Sun. With a payload capacity

designed to deliver large payloads to orbit. Falcon Heavy is one of the most powerful operational rockets in the 
world measured by liftoff thrust, with 11 launches as of March 31, 2026 and a 100% mission success rate.

questions.query: What were the 2025 year-over-year changes in Space segment revenue and cost of revenue, and what main drivers does the S-1 give for each?
questions.gold_notes: The source spells depreciation as “deprecation” in this paragraph; proof preserves the exact source spelling.

requirements.text: Space revenue increased $290 million (7.6%); launch services were relatively flat, while launch and development rose $298 million, mainly from additional NASA CRS and a U.S. Department of War contract.

quotes:
Revenue for the year ended December 31, 2025 increased by $290 million, or 7.6%, compared to the prior year 
ended December 31, 2024.  Launch Services revenue remained relatively flat year over year, while Launch and 
Development revenue increased by $298 million.  The Launch and Development revenue increase was primarily 
driven by increased revenue for an extended contract with NASA for additional Cargo Resupply Services (CRS) 
missions to the International Space Station and increased revenue from a U.S. Department of War contract.

requirements.text: Cost of revenue fell $189 million (12.2%), principally reflecting reusability and $240 million lower depreciation, with $11 million lower overhead.

quotes:
Cost of revenue for the year ended December 31, 2025 decreased by $189 million, or 12.2%, compared to the prior 
year ended December 31, 2024. This decrease was primarily due increased reusability of our Falcon launch vehicles 
resulting in lower deprecation of $240 million, lowering the cost of each launch, and lower overhead costs of $11 
million.

requirements.text: More internal Starlink launches (89 to 122) moved $14 million of launch operations and overhead into Connectivity capitalization; a $51 million inventory reserve increase partly offset the cost reduction.

quotes:
The decrease is also due to the relative increase in Starlink satellite launches from 89 launches in 2024 to 
122 launches in 2025, resulting in relatively more of our launch operations and overhead costs capitalized in our 
Connectivity segment of $14 million.  This decrease was partially offset by an increase in inventory excess and 
obsolescence reserves of $51 million mainly due to less demand on rocket vehicle and spacecraft parts as reusability 
has increased.

questions.query: How does the S-1 define a Starlink Subscriber, which customers are excluded from that metric, and how is Starlink Subscriber ARPU computed?

requirements.text: A subscriber is a unique Service Line assigned directly to a Starlink.com account without a directly negotiated agreement; it is not a count of individual people or devices.

quotes:
Starlink Subscribers: We define a Starlink Subscriber as a unique Service Line that is directly assigned to a 
Starlink.com account registered to a person or entity that does not have a direct, negotiated agreement with the 
Starlink sales team. A Service Line is an individual instance of Starlink broadband internet service provisioned 
under a subscription plan, generally associated with a specific Starlink terminal or group of terminals, and billed 
according to Starlink’s service plans and terms of service. The number of Service Lines is distinct from the number 
of unique devices, account holders, end users or physical persons.

requirements.text: Managed enterprise and government customers with negotiated contracts are excluded, including aviation, maritime, land mobility, fixed sites and government entities.

quotes:
Starlink Subscribers includes both Personal (e.g., Residential and Roam) and Business (e.g., Local 
Priority and Global Priority) subscription plans, but does not include managed enterprise and government customers 
with contracts in domains including aviation, maritime, land mobility, fixed sites and government entities.

requirements.text: ARPU equals service revenue from subscribers divided by average subscribers in the period and then by months in the period.

quotes:
Starlink Subscriber ARPU: We calculate ARPU as service revenue generated from Starlink Subscribers during the 
period divided by (i) the average number of Starlink Subscribers during the period and by (ii) the number of months 
in the period.

only users who have registered for an X or Grok account are included.
